intro: In 1325 a young man left Morocco on a donkey and spent the next thirty years crossing a world that was already connected: by camel caravans over the Sahara, by monsoon ships across the Indian Ocean, by Mongol relay roads across Asia. Two centuries later a silver coin dug from a mountain in the Andes could buy Chinese silk in the Philippines. This unit follows how the connected world of 1200 became the global world of 1750, and what that change cost the people who lived through it.

It is a story with no single hero and no single center. Song China built the richest economy on Earth. Muslim scholars kept and extended the world's science. Mali's gold paid for Italian art. Then plague crossed the same routes as silk, and a century later Europeans sailed into oceans they did not understand, met peoples they did not know existed, and set off the largest disaster and the largest forced migration in human history. Meanwhile rulers from Istanbul to Edo built states more powerful than any before them, and thinkers began to ask where a ruler's power really came from.

By the end you will be able to explain how goods, ideas and diseases traveled before and after 1492; why small Spanish forces toppled great empires; how silver and sugar tied five continents together; what the transatlantic slave trade was and how people resisted it; and how the Ottomans, Mughals, Qing, Tokugawa, Bourbons and English Parliament each answered the same question: what does a state's power rest on?
bigQuestion: How did the world become connected between 1200 and 1750, and who paid the price for those connections?

test.q: What was the foundation of Song China's economic growth?
choices: Fast-ripening rice that allowed two harvests a year
test.why: Champa rice let farmers grow more food, supporting a population of about one hundred million and freeing workers for towns.

test.q: How did the Mongol Empire affect trade across Asia?
choices: It made travel safer and faster along guarded routes and relay stations
It moved all trade to the sea
test.why: Under the Pax Mongolica, the yam relay system and Mongol protection let merchants and ideas cross Asia in weeks.

test.q: Why did trade in the Indian Ocean depend on the monsoon?
choices: The winds reversed on a predictable schedule, carrying ships out and back
The monsoon brought rain that filled the harbors
Ships could only sail during storms
test.why: Sailors timed their voyages to the summer and winter monsoons, which blew steadily in opposite directions.

test.q: What did West Africa trade across the Sahara, and for what?
test.why: West Africa had abundant gold and little salt; the desert had salt mines and needed gold, so caravans carried each toward the other.

test.q: Which was a long-term effect of the Black Death in western Europe?
choices: Wages rose and peasants gained bargaining power
test.why: With so many workers dead, survivors could demand higher pay and more freedom, and lords could not stop them.

test.q: What was Gutenberg's real contribution to printing?
choices: He invented the idea of printing
He carved the first wood blocks
He combined metal movable type, oil-based ink and a press into one system
test.why: Printing and movable type existed in Asia centuries earlier; Gutenberg's system made mass printing practical for European alphabets.

test.q: Which region was the richest and most populous in 1450?
test.why: China had the largest economy, biggest ships and oldest printing industry, though it had just ended its ocean voyages.

test.q: Why did small Spanish forces defeat the Aztec and Inca empires?
choices: The Aztec and Inca had no cities
Disease, Indigenous allies, civil war, and steel and horses combined against them
The Aztec and Inca surrendered without fighting
test.why: Smallpox, tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, an Inca civil war and Spanish weapons together explain conquests that a few hundred men could not have achieved alone.

test.q: Which food crossed from the Americas to Afro-Eurasia in the Columbian Exchange?
test.why: Potatoes, corn, tomatoes and chili peppers are American crops; wheat, sugar and coffee came from Afro-Eurasia.

test.q: Where did most silver from Potosí eventually end up?
choices: In China, exchanged for silk and other goods
test.why: China's demand for silver drew a large share of American output across the Pacific through Manila and around through Europe.

test.q: About how many Africans were forced onto slave ships between 1500 and 1866?
choices: About twelve and a half million
test.why: Ship records count roughly twelve and a half million people embarked, about ten and a half million of whom survived the crossing.

test.q: What made the transatlantic slave trade different from earlier slavery?
choices: Enslaved people were treated as inherited property and the system was tied to race
test.why: The Atlantic system was enormous, made slavery hereditary and, over time, legally tied it to African descent.

test.q: How did the printing press affect both the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution?
choices: It spread ideas and identical texts faster than authorities could stop them
It had no effect on either
test.why: Printing carried Luther's theses and Galileo's drawings across Europe in months and let scholars compare exact copies.

test.q: Which ruler abolished the tax on non-Muslims and hosted debates among faiths?
test.why: Akbar ended the jizya in 1564 and gathered Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Christians to debate at Fatehpur Sikri.

test.q: What did the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and Locke's writing of 1690 together establish?
choices: That kings rule by divine right
That the ruler is under the law and governs by the consent of the governed
That England would become a republic
test.why: Parliament's Bill of Rights limited the crown, and Locke argued that government exists to protect rights with the people's consent.

write.prompt: Make a claim: between 1200 and 1750, did the growing connections between world regions do more good or more harm for the people who lived through them? Support your claim with evidence from at least two different chapters and address the strongest evidence on the other side.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence, then say which peoples or regions you are judging by.
Use specific evidence: the Song economy, the Black Death, the Columbian Exchange, Potosí, the slave trade numbers, the printing press.
Explain your reasoning: why does each piece of evidence support your claim about good or harm?
Take the other side seriously: name the best evidence against your claim and explain why your claim still holds.
Say how we know: mention at least one kind of source, such as a traveler's account, a tax record, or archaeology.
